item.title: Notes and excerpts from the Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
item.description:
Some notes that I took down whilst reading Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass: An American Slave, an extraordinary work.

Hero of man, Odysseus himself. Man of God, infinitely divined. When one searchers for American Hero’s, here is one, completely finished. When questioned, who should we look to? The answer is short and clear - Frederic Douglass.

“What he most dreaded, that I most desired. What he most loved, that I most hated. That which to him was a great evil, to be carefully shunned, was to me a great good, to be diligently sought; and the argument which he so warmly urged, against my learning to read, only served to inspire me with a desire and determination to learn.”

item.title: Notes on Racecraft by Karen E. Fields and Barbara J. Fields
item.description:
Jotted here are some excerpts, notes and musings from Racecraft: The Soul of Inequality in American Life by the Fields’ sisters.

In addition to these scribblings, an entire chapter titled Of Rogues and Geldings is published over at Class Letter.

Ha, hilarious vindication

“Pronouncing himself “inherently gloomy about the prospects of Africa,” Watson said that “all our social policies are based on the fact that their intelligence is the same as ours—whereas testing says not really.” Indeed, in his view, reason is not properly regarded as “some universal heritage of humanity.” For evidence, however, the man of science resorted to personal impressions, haphazardly collected: “People who have to deal with black employees find this is not true.” From his digest of anecdotes, he went on to prophesy that genetic evidence for black people’s lesser intelligence would emerge within a decade.
